79954.body:

Caption: 

----------
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/3bd8a492-ff61-41db-a7f2-c821d481fd72/BD_NL_QuoteCircle.png?t=1781794162)
Caption: 

“Every stock, every bond, every fund — every asset — can be tokenized. If they are, it will revolutionize investing.”
_— __Larry Fink_



----------View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/efaad7e7-c3c6-4719-abd4-dd25cb91ba53/unnamed.png?t=1790717891)
Caption: 

# The tokenization of everything

When BlackRock’s Larry Fink says that “every asset” can be tokenized, we naturally think about stocks, bonds, and commodities — things that trade on exchanges.

But there are many more assets than that in the world — things found only on a company’s balance sheet or P&L statement, for example, like accounts receivable. Or rights encoded in legal contracts, like lease agreements.

These are incredibly valuable, of course, but the only way for an investor to get exposure is by buying a big messy bundle of them (sometimes known as a “stock”).

That might not be the only way to do it. The authors of a [research paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.11266) believe that these atomic-level assets could be traded, too — as tokens on a blockchain.

The researchers propose “a more granular approach” to tokenization, in which crypto tokens represent “a specific, independently measurable component of an asset” — a portion of a mine's output, say, or a square meter of a company's rights to use some government land.

The authors call these “Element Tokens,” and say they would be “designed to be fully collateralized by the underlying asset components.”

To help us imagine these components, they describe a diversified mining company that issues an _E_~Au ~token redeemable for a share of its output of gold (“_E_” being element and Au being the chemical symbol of gold) and an _E_~Cu~ token redeemable for a share of its output of copper.

(I’m not sure why the E is always italicized, but it does make the whole thing seem reassuringly scientific to me.)

It’s easy to see why this would be useful: Investors pay more for discrete risks than they do for a bundle of them (some of which they won’t want). Our mining company could therefore lower its cost of capital by selling _E_~Au ~tokens to investors only interested in gold and _E_~Cu~ tokens to investors only interested in copper.

But that’s not all!

The company might also issue a “land right” token — _E_~land~ — representing a claim on the company’s mines (or a single mine, even), and a “license right” toke

79948.subject: Not all revenue sharing is equal. Do buybacks beat dividends?
79948.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/27e7dada-7bb7-4fcb-8126-f9079f724579/Top_Zama.png?t=1790698426)
Follow image link: (https://defillama.com/research/report/zama-a-look-into-confidential-defi)
Caption: 

## Do buybacks or dividends perform better for DeFi tokens?

We learned 3 things from this analysis:

Analyze today’s Holders Revenue (https://defillama.com/holders-revenue?groupBy=monthly&chartView=Breakdown)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2ce13354-8950-4f20-b325-4e3e8c5c02d5/buyback-vs-dividend-tokens-ytd-return_2026-09-29__1_.png?t=1790691110)
Caption: 

1. Buyback tokens outperformed on average. +19.7% median vs +11.1% for direct distribution tokens.

2. Larger tokens performed better. Market cap vs YTD return has a strong correlation with the largest tokens in this dataset. Weighted by market cap, buyback returns explode to 190% vs direct distribution’s +29%.

3. Protocols that distribute a small portion of revenue underperformed protocols that didn’t share any revenue at all.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/27c1f501-5c76-4bab-9008-276145103480/median-ytd-return-by-revenue-retention-type_2026-09-29.png?t=1790693950)
Caption: 

A larger share of protocols distributing any revenue have positive price performance YTD compared to protocols that don’t share revenue.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/fe914896-a3e5-4483-915f-6943046b8cde/image.png?t=1790693940)
Caption: 





## The Revenue landscape transformed over the last two years

The total number of protocols with Holder Revenue has increased dramatically over the last two years.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/6ace5471-29b4-4293-89ec-bd4653579ea7/protocols-with-holder-revenue-monthly_2026-09-29.png?t=1790690570)
Caption: 

[Protocols have earned over $1b per month in total revenue](https://defillama.com/revenue?groupBy=monthly) for the last 23 months.

Holder revenue as a % of total protocol revenue is trending up. Two years ago, 5% of total protocol revenue went to holders.

After falling for the first half of this year, 15% of total protocol revenue is being distributed to holders.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/9f798dbf-8bc3-4b38-b9ef-58db69bdb0ca/holder-revenue-as-of-total-protocol-revenue_2026-09-29.png?t=1790697523)
Caption:
